flashcard_questions.q: What is a hydrocarbon compound made of?
What is the general formula of the alkanes?
Why are alkanes described as saturated hydrocarbons?
flashcard_questions.a: They contain only single covalent bonds between their carbon atoms.

flashcard_questions.q: Which alkane is the main component of natural gas?
As hydrocarbon chain length increases, what happens to the boiling point?
As hydrocarbon chain length increases, what happens to flammability?
Why do longer hydrocarbon chains have higher boiling points?
flashcard_questions.a: The intermolecular forces between the molecules are stronger.

flashcard_questions.q: Where in a fractionating column is the temperature highest?
Why do short-chain hydrocarbons condense near the top of the column?
flashcard_questions.a: They have low boiling points, so they rise further before condensing.

flashcard_questions.q: Which fraction is collected at the very bottom of the column?
Complete the word equation: hydrocarbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide + ____

flashcard_questions.a: Breaking long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful molecules.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is cracking needed at an oil refinery?
flashcard_questions.a: Demand for short-chain hydrocarbons is greater than the supply from crude oil.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the general formula of the alkenes?
What happens to orange bromine water when it is shaken with an alkene?

notes: 15 cards: 4 term→definition (hydrocarbon, saturated, cracking, viscosity trend), 2 general formula cards (alkanes, alkenes), 1 word-equation cloze for complete combustion, 3 property-trend cards written one variable at a time so answers differ, 3 fractional distillation cards (column temperature, condensation height, bitumen), 1 causal card on intermolecular forces, 1 practical test card (bromine water). Dropped the first-four-alkanes list and the incomplete combustion products as enumerations, and the two cracking methods as detail better tested by the cracking-purpose card.
